Series::equal¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

bool Series::equal(const Series& other) const

What It Does¶

Returns one C++ bool: true only when self and other have exactly the same shape and every corresponding value compares equal.

It is the whole-tensor, exact-match decision — the right tool for an assertion, a guard clause, or a container-level identity check where you want a single yes/no, not a per-element mask.

It differs from eq in two ways that matter:

  • No broadcasting. eq stretches [3] against [1, 3] and compares elementwise; equal treats any shape mismatch as an immediate false.

  • One answer, not a mask. eq returns a Bool Series; equal reduces that down to a single bool.

The comparison is on values, so operands may have different numeric dtypes and still be equal if the numbers line up (int 1 equals double 1.0). If dtype identity is also part of your requirement, check dtype().scalar separately.

There is no tolerance — equal is bit-exact-for-integers, value-exact-for-floats. For an approximate decision use allclose; for the per-position approximate mask use isclose.

Parameters¶

other (const Series&): the Series to compare against. Must be on the same platform as self when the shapes match (see Gotchas).

Returns¶

bool true iff shapes are identical and all(self == other).

Raises¶

  • if either Series is undefined

  • if the shapes match but the platforms differ

(A plain shape mismatch is not an error — it returns false.)

Gradient¶

Not applicable — equal() returns a plain bool.

Examples¶

Example 1. Exact match versus a single differing value.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "identical: " << a.equal(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0})) << "\n"
          << "one off:   " << a.equal(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0000001})) << "\n";

Output¶

identical: true
one off:   false

A difference of 1e-7 is still a difference — equal has no tolerance. If that should count as a match, you want allclose.

Example 2. Different dtype, equal values → true. equal compares numbers, not representations.

auto ints = pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3});
std::cout << "int vs float: " << std::boolalpha
          << ints.equal(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0})) << "\n";

Output¶

int vs float: true

Example 3. A shape mismatch is false immediately — no broadcasting, no error.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "[3] vs [1,3]: " << a.equal(a.unsqueeze(0)) << "\n"
          << "[3] vs [2]:   " << a.equal(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0})) << "\n";

Output¶

[3] vs [1,3]: false
[3] vs [2]:   false

[3] and [1, 3] are broadcast-compatible and eq would compare them, but they are not the same size, so equal stops at false.

Example 4. NaN never equals NaN — so equal of a tensor with a NaN against an identical copy is false.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(), 3.0});
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "equal(identical-with-NaN):      "
          << a.equal(pluss::make_series({1.0, std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(), 3.0})) << "\n"
          << "allclose(..., equal_nan=true):  "
          << a.allclose(pluss::make_series({1.0, std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(), 3.0}),
                        1e-5, 1e-8, true) << "\n";

Output¶

equal(identical-with-NaN):      false
allclose(..., equal_nan=true):  true

equal has no equal_nan option. When matching missing-value positions should count, use allclose(..., equal_nan = true).

Example 5. Two equal-shaped empty Series are equal — there is no position at which they differ.

auto e1 = pluss::series::zeros({0}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
auto e2 = pluss::series::zeros({0}, pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
std::cout << "empty [0] vs empty [0]: " << std::boolalpha << e1.equal(e2) << "\n";

Output¶

empty [0] vs empty [0]: true

Example 6. equal (one bool) versus eq (a per-element mask).

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({1.0, 9.0, 3.0});
std::cout << "a.equal(b) = " << std::boolalpha << a.equal(b) << "\n";
std::cout << "a.eq(b)    = ";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.eq(b));

Output¶

a.equal(b) = false
a.eq(b)    = Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=bool, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[true, false, true]

equal tells you whether the tensors match; eq tells you where they diverge.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • No tolerance. A 1e-12 float difference makes equal false. Use allclose for an approximate decision.

  • No broadcasting. Different shapes are false, never stretched.

  • NaN != NaN. A tensor containing NaN is never equal to any tensor, including a byte-identical copy.

  • Equal values do not imply equal dtype, layout, or shared storage — use dtype().scalar and is_set_to for those.

  • A shape mismatch returns false, but a platform mismatch on matching shapes raises — the platform check happens only after the shape check passes.

  • An undefined operand raises.

Summary¶

equal(other) is the exact, whole-tensor comparison:

  • true iff identical shape and every value equal — no tolerance, no broadcasting

  • compares values, so differing numeric dtypes can still be equal

  • NaN breaks it; equal-shaped empties satisfy it vacuously

  • use eq for the per-element mask, allclose / isclose for approximate versions
